topics.title: Adamic-Adar and resource allocation
topics.what_it_is: Adamic-Adar weights each shared neighbour by 1/log(degree). A shared rare neighbour counts more than a shared hub. Resource allocation uses 1/degree and is even stronger against hubs.
topics.why: In a KG hubs such as 'model' or 'regularization' connect everything. These scores stop hubs from creating false similarity when you propose merges or related entities.

io.inputs: A graph, two nodes.
io.outputs: A real score >= 0.

topics.trade_offs: Degree-1 common neighbours are skipped by AA (log 1 = 0). Still needs a common neighbour. In the real graph, hub pairs through 'overfitting' score low because overfitting has degree 21.

topics.title: Betweenness centrality
topics.what_it_is: Betweenness counts how often a node lies on shortest paths between other node pairs. A node with high betweenness is a bridge. Brandes (2001) computes all values in O(nm) time on unweighted graphs.
topics.why: Bridge entities connect topics. In multi-hop retrieval they are the nodes that carry a chain from one topic to another, and they are the nodes to keep when you prune a subgraph.

io.inputs: A graph, unweighted or weighted.
io.outputs: One number per node; normalised by (n-1)(n-2)/2 for undirected graphs.

symbols.sigma_st: number of shortest paths from s to t
symbols.sigma_st(v): how many of them pass through v

steps: For every pair (s,t) find all shortest paths.
For each path add 1/sigma_st to every inner node.
Normalise. Brandes does this with one BFS per source and a back-propagation of dependencies.
topics.trade_offs: Exact cost O(nm) is high for large graphs; sample sources to approximate. It counts only shortest paths, so it can miss useful longer paths. Fails on disconnected pairs (they contribute 0).

topics.title: Breadth-first search and k-hop neighbourhood
topics.what_it_is: BFS visits nodes level by level from a start node. The nodes at level k are exactly the nodes k hops away. The union of levels 0..k is the k-hop neighbourhood.
topics.why: Local GraphRAG expands from query entities by k hops (usually 1 or 2) to collect relations and passages. The size of the expansion is the main cost and noise control.

io.inputs: A graph, a seed set, a depth k.
io.outputs: The set of nodes (and edges) within k hops; each node's hop distance.

steps: Pop u; for each unvisited neighbour v set dist[v]=dist[u]+1 and push v.
topics.trade_offs: O(n+m). The neighbourhood grows fast (here 1, 19, 89, 227 nodes for 0..3 hops) so k=2 is a common cap; hubs make it explode. Without edge filtering it brings irrelevant nodes.

topics.title: Closeness centrality
topics.what_it_is: Closeness measures how near a node is to all other nodes. Take the sum of shortest-path lengths from the node, then invert it. A small sum means a central node. In a graph with separate components, scale by the share of reachable nodes (Wasserman-Faust).
topics.why: A central entity is a good seed or anchor: from it, a few hops reach most of the graph. It also helps to choose which entity summarises a community.

io.inputs: A connected (or reachable-set) graph; shortest-path distances.
io.outputs: One number per node.

symbols.r: number of nodes reachable from v, including v
symbols.note: if the graph is connected, r=n and the second factor is 1

steps: Run BFS from v to get all d(v,u).
Sum the distances over reachable nodes.
Apply the formula with the reachable count r.
topics.trade_offs: O(n(n+m)) for all nodes with BFS. Defined only inside components, so the disconnected fix matters for extracted graphs (full graph: 40 components). Values in a sparse tree-like graph are close to each other, so they rank poorly.

topics.title: Connected components
topics.what_it_is: A connected component is a maximal set of nodes where every pair has a path. Components split a graph into separate islands. A DFS or BFS labels them in linear time.
topics.why: Many extracted graphs are fragmented. Components tell you whether a path or a PPR walk can reach an entity at all, and they set the limit for global summaries (an isolated piece cannot join a bigger community).

io.inputs: A graph.
io.outputs: A component id per node and component sizes.

symbols.~: equivalence relation; its classes are the components

steps: For each unvisited node, run BFS/DFS and give every reached node the same id.
topics.trade_offs: O(n+m). For directed graphs use strongly connected components (Tarjan 1972). In an LLM-extracted KG, spelling variants break one island into many (see entity resolution, J1).

topics.title: Cosine similarity on node and text embeddings
topics.what_it_is: Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by their lengths. It measures the angle between them and ignores length. The same formula works for text embeddings and for node embeddings.
topics.why: It is the main score of vector search. For a graph, embed entity names or descriptions and use cosine to link a query phrase to graph nodes (entity linking), or compare node embeddings from node2vec/GNN.

io.inputs: Two vectors.
io.outputs: A number in [-1,1].

formulas.latex: \cos(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\frac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{\|\mathbf a\|\,\|\mathbf b\|}

steps: Normalise each vector to length 1 (many models do it already).
topics.trade_offs: For unit vectors cosine = dot product, so indexes use the dot product. It ignores magnitude, which can carry information. Different models are not comparable.

worked_example.data: Two real sentence embeddings in Presentations/_real-examples/data/vectors_sample.json (model sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, dim 384): s1 (ridge regression) and s2 (lasso).

topics.title: Degree centrality
topics.what_it_is: Degree counts how many edges touch a node. A node with many edges is a hub. Divide by n-1 to compare graphs of different size.
topics.why: A hub entity (for example 'regularization') links many passages. GraphRAG uses degree to rank entities, to cap the neighbours it expands, and to find over-general nodes that add noise.

io.inputs: A graph G=(V,E).
io.outputs: One number per node: the count of its edges, or the count divided by n-1.

steps: Count the neighbours of each node.
Divide by n-1 if you need a value between 0 and 1.
topics.trade_offs: Cheap, local, O(n+m). It ignores where the neighbours sit. A hub of weak links scores as high as a hub of strong links. Extraction noise (merged aliases, generic nodes) inflates degree.

topics.title: Shortest path (Dijkstra)
topics.what_it_is: Dijkstra finds the cheapest path from a source to all nodes when edge costs are not negative. It keeps the best known cost for every node and repeatedly settles the cheapest unsettled one.
topics.why: Path retrieval: given two entities in a question, the cheapest path is the reasoning chain you show to the LLM. Edge costs can encode relation type or evidence strength.

io.inputs: A weighted graph with costs >= 0, a source (and a target).
io.outputs: Distances and a shortest-path tree; the path from source to target.

symbols.d(v): cost of the best known path to v

steps: Pop the unsettled node u with the smallest d.
Stop when the target is settled.
topics.trade_offs: O((n+m) log n) with a heap. The result depends on the cost design. Negative costs break it. If two entities sit in different components there is no path (full graph: 40 components).

topics.title: Eigenvector centrality
topics.what_it_is: A node is important if its neighbours are important. The scores are the entries of the leading eigenvector of the adjacency matrix. Power iteration finds it.
topics.why: It rewards a node that sits among other hubs. It is the idea behind PageRank (a damped, normalised variant) and gives a second way to rank entities for seed selection.

io.inputs: A connected graph (use the largest component).
io.outputs: One non-negative score per node, scaled so the vector has unit length.

steps: Repeat x <- A x, then divide by its norm.
Stop when x no longer changes.
topics.trade_offs: Needs a connected graph; on disconnected graphs the score concentrates in the largest component. Hubs can pass all their weight to a few neighbours. On bipartite graphs power iteration can oscillate.

topics.title: Graph attention network (GAT)
topics.what_it_is: A GAT layer learns how much each neighbour matters. For a node, it scores every neighbour with a small network, turns the scores into weights with softmax, and takes the weighted sum of neighbour features.
topics.why: Attention weights show which neighbours the model uses, so the retrieved subgraph can be explained. GNN retrievers use attention to weight KG edges for a question.

io.inputs: Node features, weight matrix W, attention vector a.
io.outputs: New node features and attention weights alpha_ij.

formulas.latex: e_{ij}=\mathrm{LeakyReLU}\bigl(\mathbf a^{\top}[W\mathbf h_i\Vert W\mathbf h_j]\bigr),\quad\alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp e_{ij}}{\sum_{k\in N(i)}\exp e_{ik}},\quad\mathbf h_i'=\sigma\Bigl(\sum_{j}\alpha_{ij}W\mathbf h_j\Bigr)

symbols.alpha_ij: attention weight of neighbour j for node i (sums to 1 over j)

steps: Score each neighbour (and the node itself).
topics.trade_offs: Illustration only: W and a are random (numpy seed 0), not trained, so the weights carry no meaning; they show the mechanics and that they sum to 1. Multi-head attention is used in practice. Cost per layer is O(m d).

topics.title: Graph convolutional network (GCN)
topics.what_it_is: A GCN layer averages the feature vectors of a node and its neighbours with a symmetric degree normalisation, then multiplies by a weight matrix and applies a non-linearity.
topics.why: GCN is the simplest practical GNN. It shows how a node's representation blends its own and its neighbours' features, which is also how GNN-based retrievers score KG nodes.

io.inputs: Adjacency A, node features X, weights W.
io.outputs: New node features H'.

topics.trade_offs: Fixed averaging: all neighbours count the same (GAT learns weights). Transductive. Features here are one-hot node types with W=identity and no non-linearity, so no learning is shown, only the propagation step.

topics.title: HITS (hubs and authorities)
topics.what_it_is: HITS gives every node two scores. A good authority is pointed to by good hubs. A good hub points to good authorities. Iterate the two rules until they settle.
topics.why: On typed, directed KG edges it separates nodes that others point to (defining concepts) from nodes that point to many (survey-like entities). It is rarely used in GraphRAG; it is a useful contrast to PageRank.

io.inputs: A directed graph.
io.outputs: A hub score and an authority score per node.

steps: a <- A^T h, normalise; h <- A a, normalise.
Repeat to convergence (principal singular vectors of A).
topics.trade_offs: Query-dependent in the original (it runs on a focused subgraph). Sensitive to tightly linked clusters. Needs edge direction; extracted relations have arbitrary direction ('uses', 'part_of'), which limits meaning.

topics.title: Node similarity: common neighbours and Jaccard
topics.what_it_is: Two nodes are similar if they share many neighbours. Common neighbours counts them. Jaccard divides by the size of the union of the two neighbour sets, so large neighbourhoods do not win just by size.
topics.why: Use it to merge duplicate entities (entity resolution), to find related entities for query expansion, and as the base of link prediction.

io.inputs: A graph and two nodes u, v.
io.outputs: A score in [0,1] (Jaccard) or an integer count (common neighbours).

topics.title: Label propagation
topics.what_it_is: Each node starts with its own label. In every round, a node takes the label that most of its neighbours have. Labels spread until each node agrees with the majority of its neighbours. The labels are the communities.
topics.why: It is a very cheap way to find communities on huge graphs. It is also a baseline for Leiden.

io.inputs: An undirected graph.
io.outputs: A community label per node.

steps: Give each node a unique label.
In random order, set each node's label to the neighbour majority.
Stop when every node has a majority label.
topics.trade_offs: Near linear time, but not deterministic: different seeds give different partitions, and it can leave many tiny communities. No quality function is optimised.

topics.title: Leiden community detection
topics.what_it_is: Leiden improves Louvain by adding a refinement step. After local moving, it splits each community into well-connected sub-parts before aggregating. It guarantees connected communities and converges to a stable partition.
topics.why: Microsoft GraphRAG runs Leiden on the entity graph to get hierarchical communities, then writes an LLM report per community for global search. The repo's run: 57 communities, Q 0.8505.

io.inputs: An undirected (weighted) graph, quality function (modularity or CPM), resolution.
io.outputs: A hierarchy of node partitions, each community connected.

formulas.latex: \text{same quality }Q\text{ as Louvain; adds refinement: merge a node into a sub-community only if it is well connected (}\theta\text{-randomised)}

steps: Refine the partition inside each community.
Aggregate on the refined partition (initial = non-refined).
topics.trade_offs: Needs igraph/leidenalg. Still a heuristic. Small communities may be only singletons; GraphRAG summarises only communities above a size. Resolution parameter changes level sizes.

topics.title: Link prediction
topics.what_it_is: Link prediction scores node pairs that have no edge and asks which one is likely to be a missing or future edge. The scores are the similarity measures of the previous entries, or the output of a model.
topics.why: LLM-built graphs miss edges. Link prediction proposes missing relations, ranks candidate edges for repair, and evaluates how well a graph structure predicts held-out relations.

topics.title: Louvain community detection
topics.what_it_is: Louvain greedily maximises modularity in two repeated steps. Step 1: move each node to the neighbouring community that raises Q most. Step 2: merge each community into one super-node and repeat on the smaller graph.
topics.why: It is fast enough for large graphs and gives a hierarchy. Many GraphRAG pipelines used it before Leiden.

io.inputs: An undirected graph.
io.outputs: A partition and a hierarchy of partitions.

steps: Local moving until no move raises Q.
topics.trade_offs: Can produce badly connected or even disconnected communities (Traag et al. 2019, the reason for Leiden). Result depends on node order and seed.

steps: Compute a message from every neighbour.
Update the node with a small network.
topics.trade_offs: Over-smoothing: deep stacks make all nodes similar. Over-squashing on long paths. Needs training data and features. Cost grows with neighbourhood size (neighbour sampling).

topics.title: Modularity
topics.what_it_is: Modularity Q measures how good a split of the graph into communities is. It compares the share of edges inside communities with the share expected if edges were placed at random with the same degrees. Higher is better.
topics.why: Leiden and Louvain maximise it. Microsoft GraphRAG builds its community hierarchy this way, so Q tells you how clean the partition is before you summarise it.

io.inputs: A graph and a partition of its nodes.
io.outputs: A number in [-0.5, 1).

steps: For each community compute L_c/m and (K_c/2m)^2.
topics.trade_offs: Resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthelemy 2007, not looked up): tiny communities merge. Q depends on graph size, so compare partitions of the same graph. The repo's Leiden partition has Q=0.8505 on 57 communities.

topics.why: Node embeddings let vector search work on graph structure. They support link prediction, node classification and entity similarity with no text. In GraphRAG they can feed a retriever or a GNN as node features.

io.outputs: One vector per node.

topics.trade_offs: Training not run here (only the walk step). Embeddings are transductive: a new node needs re-training (GraphSAGE fixes this). p and q need tuning per graph. Static: edges added later do not update vectors.

topics.title: PageRank
topics.what_it_is: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows an edge with probability d and jumps to a random node with probability 1-d. A node is important if important nodes link to it.
topics.why: It ranks entities by global importance. It is the base of Personalized PageRank, which HippoRAG and other GraphRAG systems use to spread relevance from query entities.

io.inputs: A directed or undirected graph, damping d (usually 0.85).
io.outputs: One probability per node; the probabilities sum to 1.

symbols.note: Normalised form used by networkx (sums to 1). Page et al. (1999, Sec. 2.4) write R'(u)=c*sum_{v in B_u} R'(v)/N_v + c*E(u) with ||E||_1=0.15; Brin & Page (1998) write PR(A)=(1-d)+d*sum PR(T_i)/C(T_i), which sums to N, not 1.

steps: Repeat p <- d P p + (1-d)/n until the L1 change is tiny.
Send the weight of dangling nodes (no edges) to a uniform (or personalisation) vector.
topics.trade_offs: Power iteration O(k(n+m)). On extracted entity graphs, edges have no 'vote' meaning, so global PageRank mostly echoes degree. Choice of d changes ranks. Isolated nodes keep only the teleport mass.

topics.title: Prize-collecting Steiner tree (PCST)
topics.what_it_is: PCST picks a tree in the graph. Nodes have prizes (how relevant they are). Edges have costs. The tree maximises the total prize minus the total edge cost. The result is a small connected subgraph that includes the relevant nodes and drops the rest.
topics.why: G-Retriever uses PCST to cut a large KG down to a connected, query-focused subgraph that fits the LLM prompt. It keeps the bridge nodes that connect the relevant ones.

io.inputs: A graph, node prizes, edge costs.
io.outputs: A connected subtree (nodes and edges).

formulas.latex: S^*=\arg\max_{S\subseteq G\text{ connected}}\sum_{n\in V_S}prize(n)+\sum_{e\in E_S}prize(e)-|E_S|\,C_e,\quad prize(n)=k-i\ \text{for the top-}i\text{ node}

symbols.k: number of top nodes/edges that receive a prize

steps: Set prizes from retrieval scores (G-Retriever: top-k nodes get prizes by rank).
topics.trade_offs: NP-hard; Goemans-Williamson gives a 2-approximation. Prize and cost scale decide the size of the output. Needs a connected region around the prizes; a prize node in another component is lost.

topics.title: Personalized PageRank (PPR)
topics.what_it_is: PPR is PageRank with the jump going back to chosen seed nodes. The score of a node is the chance that a random walk that restarts at the seeds is at that node. Nodes close to the seeds in many ways get high scores.
topics.why: HippoRAG seeds PPR with the entities found in the query and ranks passages by the node scores. It finds multi-hop context that a vector search misses.

io.inputs: A graph, seed set S with weights, restart probability.
io.outputs: A score per node; the top nodes (then their passages) are the retrieved context.

symbols.alpha: probability to continue the walk (networkx 'alpha'); restart probability is 1-alpha

steps: Detect query entities (entity linking) and set s.
Run power iteration or solve the linear system.
Sort nodes by r; map top nodes to passages.
topics.trade_offs: A larger alpha spreads further from the seeds; the repo uses restart 0.5. Hub nodes soak up mass, so dense hubs can crowd out the answer. The repo's measured run: PPR graph R@5 0.775 and MRR 0.756 versus dense 0.85 / 0.917 on 24 questions, so PPR alone did not beat vectors there.

topics.title: Random walk with restart (RWR)
topics.what_it_is: RWR is a random walk that, at each step, goes back to the start node with probability c. The stationary distribution scores how close every node is to the start in the whole graph, not just along one shortest path.
topics.why: It is the proximity measure behind PPR-style retrieval: it counts many short routes, so multi-hop evidence that is reachable in several ways scores higher.

io.inputs: A graph, a start node, restart probability c.
io.outputs: A proximity score per node.

symbols.e: unit vector for the start node

steps: Iterate r <- (1-c) A~ r + c e to convergence, or solve the linear system.
topics.trade_offs: Same maths as PPR with a single seed (c = 1 - alpha). Tong et al. add fast approximations for large graphs (block elimination, low rank).

topics.title: Steiner tree
topics.what_it_is: A Steiner tree is the cheapest tree that connects a given set of terminal nodes, and it may use extra nodes (Steiner nodes). With unit costs it is the connected subgraph with the fewest edges that contains all terminals.
topics.why: Given the entities in a multi-hop question, the Steiner tree is the minimal connected evidence subgraph. It shows the intermediate entities that tie the terminals together.

io.inputs: A graph with edge costs and a terminal set.
io.outputs: A tree with minimum total cost.

steps: Build the metric closure on the terminals (shortest paths).
Expand the MST edges into paths and prune.
topics.trade_offs: NP-hard (Karp 1972). The KMB heuristic is within factor 2 of the optimum. Terminals in different components have no Steiner tree.

topics.title: Subgraph extraction (ego graph and induced subgraph)
topics.what_it_is: Subgraph extraction cuts out the part of the graph that matters for a query. An ego graph is the k-hop neighbourhood of a node. An induced subgraph keeps a chosen node set and all edges between them.
topics.why: This is the step that decides what the LLM reads. Local GraphRAG takes an ego graph around the linked entities. G-Retriever tightens it with PCST. SubgraphRAG and GNN-RAG score and prune edges.

io.inputs: A graph, seed nodes, extraction rule.
io.outputs: A small graph with its nodes, edges and linked passages.

steps: Expand by k hops or by score.
Serialise to text for the prompt.
topics.trade_offs: Size explodes (see k-hop). A fixed k mixes relevant and irrelevant nodes. Pruning by PPR or by PCST trades recall for prompt length.

topics.title: Which graph algorithm for which GraphRAG job
topics.what_it_is: This map links each graph algorithm to its job in a GraphRAG system: ranking entities, spreading relevance from a query, building communities for global answers, merging duplicates, choosing a subgraph, and learning node vectors.
topics.why: It answers the question 'what is the algorithm for, and what does its result mean here'. It gives the reader the right entry point.

io.inputs: A GraphRAG pipeline stage.
io.outputs: A choice of algorithm.

steps: Name the job (rank, expand, group, merge, cut, embed).
Use the table in the numbers field.
topics.trade_offs: The mapping is our synthesis from the papers listed (inferred where no paper states it). Systems differ: LightRAG uses no community detection; HippoRAG uses PPR; Microsoft GraphRAG uses Leiden; G-Retriever uses PCST.
